stories.title: The autistic brain processes faces differently than scientists thought
summary: A major new study reveals that autistic children’s brains process faces differently, and those differences may begin earlier than scientists previously thought.
Researchers found that brain signals associated with recognizing faces become more specialized as neurotypical children grow older, but show much less change in autistic children.
The discovery could help explain why some autistic people have difficulty recognizing faces and reading emotions.

stories.title: The asteroid that killed the dinosaurs may have helped ants conquer the world
summary: The asteroid that killed the dinosaurs may have set the stage for ants to conquer the planet, with a surprising boost from “jumping genes” hidden in their DNA.

Scientists discovered that bursts of activity from these mobile genetic elements coincided with the rise of major ant groups and may have helped sharpen their extraordinary ability to communicate through smell.

stories.title: A bust-up between mathematicians is fuelling fears that AI could undermine science
summary: AI has made some awesome scientific discoveries.
But now, questions are being raised about its accuracy

stories.title: Scientists discover the immune system’s hidden sense of touch
summary: Scientists at McGill University have discovered a surprising new ability of immune cells that could change how we understand long-term immunity.

Researchers found that T cells can actually sense how stiff their surrounding tissues are, using these physical signals to help determine whether they develop into long-lasting memory cells that protect against future infections.

stories.title: Weather warning lifted as third storm to hit Scotland eases off
summary: Energy provider SSEN says 2,000 properties in the north of Scotland are still without power after days of high winds and heavy rain.

stories.title: Will a new strategy help protect Northern Ireland's nature?
summary: About 40% of the plants and animals in protected sites across Northern Ireland fall short of meeting the standard for "favourable condition".

stories.title: Tiny zebra-striped bee sighting a 'huge surprise'
summary: A zebra-striped bee is seen in Somerset for the first time, offering hope in restored saltmarshes.

stories.title: Scotland's recycling rates at five-year low. How is your area doing?
summary: Environmental regulator Sepa says households recycled 42.8% of waste in 2025 - down from 44.3% the previous year.

stories.title: What's happening to our rubbish?
summary: As Scotland's recycling rate falls to its lowest level in five years, Kevin Keane looks at what happens to our rubbish.

stories.title: Wildlife appeal closes in on £30m target
summary: The government pledges £1.9m to wildlife groups' efforts to buy the Rothbury Estate.

stories.title: Regular spaceplane flights planned in project
summary: Spaceplanes could take off on regular flights from Cornwall following an agreement.

stories.title: Common drugs may help dangerous viruses spread through the body
summary: A surprising discovery reveals that widely used anti-inflammatory drugs may unintentionally help dangerous viruses spread through the body.
Scientists found that JAK inhibitors, prescribed for rheumatoid arthritis and other inflammatory diseases, can weaken a crucial immune defense against influenza, COVID-19, and other infections.
By suppressing genes that normally fight viruses, these medications may leave patients more vulnerable to infection.

stories.title: What is Nasa's Artemis III mission? And what comes next?
summary: Artemis III will help test crucial systems needed for the planned Artemis IV Moon landing in 2028.

stories.title: More high winds hit parts of UK as Storm Boelo clean-up continues
summary: A Met Office weather warning is in place for Scotland and Northern Ireland for much of Tuesday.

stories.title: James Webb discovers a scorching lava planet with a “giant sunscreen”
summary: A scorching lava planet 280 light-years away has surprised astronomers by apparently maintaining a thick atmosphere despite conditions that should have stripped it away billions of years ago.
James Webb Space Telescope observations suggest that TOI-561 b reflects about 75% of incoming starlight, possibly because of mineral clouds that act like a giant sunscreen.
The planet may also be continually replenishing its atmosphere through gases released from a global ocean of molten rock.

stories.title: Smithsonian scientists just recreated the first 2 billion years of the Universe
summary: Scientists have created one of the largest and most detailed simulations of the early universe ever made, offering an extraordinary new glimpse into the cosmos shortly after the Big Bang.

Called Lumina, the groundbreaking simulation recreates the universe’s first 2 billion years, showing how dark matter, gas, and radiation interacted to give rise to the earliest stars, galaxies, and black holes.

stories.title: Do spiders dream? Scientists just found a surprising clue
summary: Scientists have discovered that spiders may sleep in ways surprisingly similar to humans, complete with distinct sleep stages and a dream-like REM state.
Researchers at the University of Bonn studied the Australian jumping spider Portia fimbriata, a remarkably clever hunter known for its sophisticated strategies.
By recording the spiders over several days and nights, they found clear evidence of regulated sleep, including a REM-like stage marked by eye movements and muscle twitches.

stories.title: Scientists discover a surprising clue to why some brains resist Alzheimer’s
summary: Why do some people stay mentally sharp even when their brains show signs of Alzheimer’s disease?
Scientists in the Netherlands may have uncovered an important clue hidden in a rare group of immature brain cells.
Researchers discovered that these cells remain present even in people over 80, but their behavior differs dramatically between those who develop dementia and those who remain cognitively healthy.

stories.title: Mayo Clinic discovers new ways to fight the “zombie” cells that drive aging
summary: Mayo Clinic scientists have uncovered surprising new insights into “zombie cells,” aging cells that linger in the body and contribute to inflammation and disease.
In aging mice, experimental treatments reduced inflammation and improved physical and brain health.
The findings could open the door to therapies that combat some of the biological processes behind aging.

stories.title: 1.9-million-year-old discovery rewrites the story of human evolution
summary: New evidence suggests that early humans reached the Jordan Valley at least 1.9 million years ago, hundreds of thousands of years earlier than scientists previously thought.
Advanced dating methods revealed that the ‘Ubeidiya site is roughly as old as the famous Dmanisi site in Georgia, placing both among the earliest known human settlements outside Africa.

stories.title: Scientists solve a 30-year mystery behind inflammatory bowel disease
summary: Scientists have identified a hidden cause of inflammatory bowel disease: antibodies that disable the immune system’s natural ability to control inflammation, potentially explaining severe illness in thousands of patients.
The breakthrough also solves a 30-year genetic mystery and could pave the way for more precise diagnoses and targeted treatments.
